observation.visible_scene: A high-speed close-up of a male hummingbird with a brilliant magenta-red gorget perched on a thin horizontal twig against a pure black background. The bird's head and breast carry clinging water droplets, and numerous separate droplets hang suspended in the air around it. Its wings are spread to either side and rendered as motion-blurred streaks. A yellow National Geographic logo sits in the upper-right corner throughout.
visible_changes: The bird's body remains fixed on the same spot of the twig from first to last frame; only the head moves.

The head continuously rotates and tilts: the dark beak sweeps from pointing down-and-right in the early frames, to pointing right, then up-and-outward in the middle frames, and finally up-and-left in the later frames, indicating an ongoing head-shaking motion already in progress at t=0.
Water droplets sitting on the crown and face travel with the rotating head, shifting position relative to the eye and beak base.

A distinct free droplet at the lower-left edge of the breast drifts steadily downward and leftward across the sequence (roughly from mid-chest in frame 1 to well below the twig line by the last frame), separating from the bird.
The blurred wings stay extended laterally the whole time, their streak orientation shifting slightly with the body/head motion but never folding in.
Background airborne droplets remain scattered, with only small positional differences between frames, consistent with near-static suspension in the slow-motion capture.
The framing and the twig's vertical position stay constant, showing no detectable camera pan or zoom.
outside_clip_unknowns: What initially wetted the bird (rain, a splash, or a prior shake) is not shown.
Whether the shaking and droplet shedding continue after the last frame or stop is not shown.
The exact moment the head-shake began lies before this cropped segment.
uncertain_details: Whether the blurred wings are actively flapping or are simply motion-blurred by the body shake cannot be resolved from the streaks.
The cause of each free droplet's motion (gravity versus being flung by the shake) is not directly observable.
Minor apparent shifts of background droplets may be real motion or frame-to-frame focus/bokeh differences.
